items.followUp: Does iron rust? Explain how rusting can be prevented.

rubric.why: Identifies the protective oxide coating formed on aluminium.
rubric.description: Explains the protective coating on aluminium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that aluminium forms a thin, protective aluminium oxide layer.

rubric.why: Clarifies why aluminium does not continue to corrode like iron.
rubric.description: Explains why aluminium does not rust.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the coating prevents further corrosion; accept that rust is specifically the corrosion product of iron.

modelAnswer: Aluminium does not rust; rust is the name for the corrosion product of iron.
Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide, which prevents further corrosion.

items.followUp: Write down two physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Rewards one correct physical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct physical property, such as lustre, malleability, ductility or good conductivity.

rubric.why: Rewards a second distinct correct physical property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct correct physical property of metals.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous (shiny).
Metals are malleable and can be hammered into sheets.

items.followUp: Write down two uses of copper.

rubric.why: Recognises one valid use of gold.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid use, such as making jewellery, ornaments or coins, or use in electronics or dentistry.

rubric.why: Recognises a second valid use of gold.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct valid use of gold.

modelAnswer: Gold is used to make jewellery and ornaments.
Gold is also used in coins and in electronic components.

items.followUp: Complete and balance the equation: Ca + Cl₂ → …

rubric.why: Checks that the correct product, magnesium nitride, is identified.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for writing Mg₃N₂ as the product.

rubric.why: Checks that the equation is balanced with the correct coefficients.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the balanced equation 3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂.

modelAnswer: The product is magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂.
3Mg + N₂ → Mg₃N₂

items.followUp: Define a compound. Differentiate between an atom and a molecule.

rubric.why: Checks the defining idea that an element contains only one kind of atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining an element as a pure substance made of only one kind of atom.

rubric.why: Checks that a molecule is a neutral group of atoms.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating that a molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.

rubric.why: Checks that a molecular ion is a charged group of atoms.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for defining a molecular ion as a charged group of atoms; an example such as NH₄⁺ or SO₄²⁻ may support the definition.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical means.
A molecule is an electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
A molecular ion is a group of two or more atoms carrying an overall positive or negative charge.
Examples of molecular ions are NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻.

items.followUp: What is meant by atomic number? State the rules for filling electrons into shells of an atom.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of electronic configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as the arrangement or distribution of electrons in the shells of an atom.

rubric.why: Checks the shell-capacity rule.
rubric.description: Maximum electron capacity of a shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n².

rubric.why: Checks that electrons fill shells in order from the inside outward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that inner shells are filled before outer shells.

rubric.why: Checks the limit on electrons in the outermost shell used in basic configurations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the outermost shell generally contains a maximum of 8 electrons (the first shell holds a maximum of 2).

modelAnswer: Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom.
The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n², where n is the shell number.
Electrons fill the shells successively, starting with the innermost shell.
The outermost shell generally contains no more than 8 electrons; the first shell can contain no more than 2.

items.followUp: Explain single and triple covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks that a single covalent bond involves sharing one pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for explaining that one pair of electrons is shared between two atoms to form a single covalent bond; accept a correct example such as H₂ or Cl₂.

rubric.why: Checks that a double covalent bond involves sharing two pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for explaining that two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms to form a double covalent bond; accept a correct example such as O₂.

rubric.why: Checks the conventional representation of the bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or correctly showing that a single bond is represented by one line and a double bond by two lines.

modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
It is represented by one line; for example, H—H in a hydrogen molecule.
A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
It is represented by two lines; for example, O=O in an oxygen molecule.
In both cases, sharing electrons helps the atoms attain stable outer shells.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature and particle size affect the rate of diffusion in liquids.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on particle motion and diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that higher temperature increases particle kinetic energy and makes diffusion faster.

rubric.why: Checks how the concentration difference affects diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a greater concentration difference or gradient increases the rate of diffusion.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of particle size on diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that smaller particles diffuse faster than larger particles.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of the liquid medium's resistance to flow.
rubric.description: Effect of viscosity of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that diffusion is faster in a less viscous liquid and slower in a more viscous liquid.

modelAnswer: Higher temperature gives liquid particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and diffuse more rapidly.
A greater concentration difference between two regions increases the rate of diffusion.
Smaller particles diffuse faster than larger particles.
Diffusion is faster in a less viscous liquid and slower in a more viscous liquid.
